cards.title: Build a Tech Pack Before Contacting Any Factory
cards.summary: A tech pack is the product blueprint that stops factories from guessing on materials, colors, measurements and packaging, which is the root cause of inconsistent shipments.
cards.use_when: You are preparing to source a new physical product or reorder an existing one and need to lock specifications before requesting factory quotes.
steps: Draft a single document that defines exactly how the product must be built, from materials through packaging. Factories optimize for throughput, not your brand, so anything undefined gets replaced with whatever is easiest for them.

Include: detailed product drawings or photos from every angle; exact materials and finishes including GSM, trims and hardware; measurements for every size or variant; colorways with Pantone codes; label, packaging and care instructions; and a clear product name, version and date.
If you are not a designer, hire one. The source notes experienced product designers on Upwork can build a tech pack for around $200, and calls it worth the cost.
Keep specs current using Figma, Canva or Notion templates so every reorder references the same version.
Treat every reorder as a gamble until a tech pack exists: without it you may get lucky once but cannot build consistency across orders.
caveats: Tech pack cost and freelancer availability are the source's example, not a guaranteed price. Verify current marketplace rates.

The source's cautionary example is a blanket brand that received three different shades of gray and different weights in one SKU because no spec sheet was ever sent — results are illustrative, not a benchmark.

cards.title: Shortlist and Vet Suppliers on Alibaba Before Committing
cards.summary: Treat Alibaba as a research tool: filter verified suppliers, message 10-15 factories, then verify with video calls and certification checks before shortlisting.
cards.use_when: You have a tech pack ready and need to find and screen candidate factories for a new product or a new category.
steps: Search by your exact product type and filter for verified suppliers and trade assurance. Do not click the first professional-looking listing.
Message at least 10 to 15 factories. Expect some to drop out — you are testing responsiveness, professionalism, and whether they have produced similar products before.

Get on video calls with shortlisted factories. Ask them to walk you through their facility or show sample products. Red flags: vague answers, poor communication, or visibly operating from a living room.
Verify tenure, export countries, and request documents such as ISO or BSCI certifications.
If scaling, consider a sourcing agent or platform that inspects factories in person on your behalf.
Consider diversifying beyond China — Vietnam, India and Turkey are options — but the source says this suits more established businesses at the right size, so assess whether you are there yet.
caveats: The source calls Alibaba 'totally fine' for pricing, materials and MOQ research but explicitly says to treat it as research, not a final decision.
Country diversification advice is qualified by business maturity, not a universal recommendation.

cards.title: Request a Structured Quote Before Sampling
cards.summary: A complete quote request forces suppliers to commit on unit cost, MOQ, lead time, packaging and payment terms so factories are comparable side by side.
cards.use_when: You have a shortlist of vetted factories and need comparable commercial terms to choose between them or use as negotiation leverage.
steps: Send your tech pack to each shortlisted factory with a request for a quote covering all of the following, not just unit price.
Ask for unit cost broken out per SKU or variation.
Ask for minimum order quantity per SKU.
Ask for lead time to manufacture, in days.
Ask for packaging details and specifications.
Ask for payment terms.
Use the resulting quotes from at least one other supplier as leverage: the source states no factory will lower price or improve payment terms unless they know you have options.
caveats: The source does not specify a standard payment-term structure, so negotiate based on what protects your cash flow.
Getting a competing quote is described as leverage, but the source also warns against hostile squeezing of suppliers.

cards.title: Run the Sample Progression: Strike-Off to Pre-Production to Production
cards.summary: Advance through three sample stages and hold a factory sample as the gold standard reference so bulk orders can be checked against it.
cards.use_when: You are selecting between final candidate factories or preparing to green-light bulk production.
steps: Order samples from every potential supplier you are considering — this tests communication and reliability as much as quality. Watch who follows instructions, sends updates unprompted, and matches your tech pack precisely.
Start with a strike-off or small test sample to approve materials and prints.
Move to a pre-production sample that should match your tech pack perfectly. Treat this as the gold standard you will compare bulk against.
For apparel, confirm grading here: get multiple pre-production samples to verify sizes scale correctly (S, M, L proportions).
Keep one approved sample in-house and one at the factory for reference.
After choosing the final supplier, order a production sample built right before mass production. If it does not match the pre-production standard, do not proceed.
Protect your IP as you scale: keep original tech packs, artwork and source files on your side, sign a manufacturing agreement at volume, and register trademarks.
caveats: The source presents the production sample mismatch as a hard stop; it does not discuss scenarios where minor deviation might be acceptable.
Grading guidance is specific to apparel sizing.

cards.title: Calculate True Landed Cost Instead of X-Factory Price
cards.summary: The supplier quote is only the X-factory price; landed cost adds freight, duties, taxes, insurance, warehousing, platform fees and 3PL pick/pack to reveal real per-unit profitability.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether a product is viable, setting retail price, or evaluating a supplier quote before committing to a production run.
steps: Treat the factory quote as the X-factory price covering only physical production. Do not use it for margin decisions.

Build a detailed spreadsheet listing every cost layer: product, freight, packaging, duties, taxes, insurance, warehousing, 3PL fulfillment/pick-pack fees, platform fees, transaction costs and payment transfer fees.
If you sell to customers via courier, add courier fees to understand the full landed cost to the customer.
Run the numbers before manufacturing, not after. The source describes rushing from design to manufacturing without checking numbers as the mistake larger companies make too.
Use the landed cost to inform ad spend, offer strategy, pricing and negotiation — the source stresses this is the only number that matters in sourcing.
To sanity-check your spreadsheet, the source suggests prompting a general AI chatbot to list hidden cost categories, then filling out a template. Verify each line item against your actual invoices.
caveats: The source's illustration is a hypothetical heated-pocket product: costing $40 to make would require selling near $200 at a $50 target — the logic is directional, not a pricing formula.
Freight fluctuates with fuel and global shipping rates, and duties vary by country and product type, so landed cost must be recalculated periodically.

cards.title: Prioritize Flexibility Over Lowest Unit Cost in Early Production Runs
cards.summary: Chasing the cheapest unit price early can trap cash in unsold inventory; early runs are for learning velocity, quality consistency and delay patterns before negotiating hard.
cards.use_when: You are negotiating your first few production runs and deciding between a cheaper large order and a pricier smaller one.
steps: Recognize that saving a small amount per unit by overcommitting can kill cash flow. The source describes founders who saved $2 a unit but ended with warehouses of unsold product.
In early runs, accept slightly higher per-unit cost to preserve room to test, pivot and adjust order sizes.
Use the first runs to answer: how fast does stock sell, how consistent is quality, where do delays happen.
Once you have those answers, negotiate with real data — share your forecast and demonstrate you are serious about scaling.
Negotiate for partnership, not maximum extraction. Squeezing a supplier too hard invites cheaper materials, skipped quality control or slower timelines.
Get quotes or samples from at least one other supplier to keep the conversation honest without hostility.
caveats: This is the source's explicit position that early flexibility is worth more than margin; it may not apply once volume and demand are proven.
The $2-per-unit example is illustrative, not a rule about acceptable cost premiums.

cards.title: Choose Air vs Sea Freight with a Hybrid Strategy
cards.summary: Blend air freight for speed and sea freight for margin, choosing based on product size, weight and urgency rather than always taking the cheapest rate.
cards.use_when: You are planning how to move a finished production run from factory to warehouse.
steps: Air is fast and expensive — suited to small, urgent batches or very small products.
Sea freight is slower but dramatically cheaper and keeps margins healthy at scale.
Most successful brands the source describes use a hybrid: air a small batch to start selling quickly, then follow with sea shipments to restock at lower cost.
Adjust to product characteristics: small items suit a mix; large or heavy items almost always favor sea.

Plan lead times backwards. Sea can take 30-40 days door-to-door, air 7-10 days, and production itself adds roughly 20-30 days. If you wait until you are nearly out of stock to reorder, you are already late.
Start planning the next shipment the moment your current one lands.

Use a freight forwarder for container booking, customs and delivery coordination. Do not simply chase the cheapest forwarder — the source warns the cheapest may leave goods sitting at port for weeks to fill a container.
caveats: Transit and production day ranges are the source's typical estimates, not guarantees; confirm current lead times with your forwarder.
The source notes freight forwarders quote based on route, weight and deadlines.

cards.title: Book a Pre-Shipment QC Inspection Before the Container Leaves
cards.summary: A third-party QC inspection before shipment catches defects while the factory can still fix them; once goods are on the water, problems cannot be corrected.
cards.use_when: A production run is finishing at the factory and you are about to approve final payment and shipment.
steps: Before the container leaves the factory, book a third-party quality control inspection.
The source cites a rough cost of about $200 per inspection, framing it as insurance against far larger losses from damaged or inconsistent stock.
Have the QC agent test random units, check measurements, verify packaging and labeling, and check carton weight.
Require the agent to photograph everything and flag even small inconsistencies that could become larger issues later.
If problems are found, the factory fixes them before the shipment departs.
Approve or reject the shipment based on the QC report and release final payment only once everything passes.
caveats: The $200 cost and a '$20,000 saved' figure are the source's illustrative numbers, not validated benchmarks; get current quotes from inspection providers.
The source frames the inspection as effectively mandatory before shipment.

cards.title: Select a 3PL with Documented Accuracy, Speed, Communication and Scalability
cards.summary: Fulfillment partners fail under peak volume; evaluate 3PLs on error rate, peak throughput, direct contacts and prior Q4 surge handling — and visit the warehouse.
cards.use_when: You are choosing or replacing a 3PL to store, pick, pack and ship orders, or evaluating whether your current one can handle forecast peak volume.
steps: Do not compare only on price or promises. Ask about accuracy: what is their error rate on orders shipped?
Ask about speed: how fast do they process during peak volume and how do they achieve it?
Ask about communication: who is your direct contact when problems actually hit?
Ask about scalability: how have they handled previous Q4 surges for other brands?
Ask how they handle returns, damages and restocks, and whether they flag issues proactively or wait for you to notice.
Visit the warehouse in person. The source says after touring two or three, you can tell who the real operators are.
Once running, treat fulfillment as a living system: track inventory turnover weekly, maintain shared dashboards with the warehouse, and hold monthly reviews with your 3PL.
caveats: The source's cautionary example — a 3PL collapsing during a Q4 forecast of $45-50M in sales, causing tens of millions in lost revenue and public customer complaints — is illustrative of risk, not a typical outcome.
The source notes 3PLs often integrate directly with Shopify or warehouse management tools; verify integration compatibility with your current stack.

cards.title: Calculate Reorder Point with Velocity, Lead Time and Safety Stock
cards.summary: Reorder Point = (Daily Sales Velocity x Total Lead Time) + Safety Stock, so you reorder before running dry rather than chasing demand.
cards.use_when: You are setting reorder triggers and planning replenishment shipments for any SKU.
steps: Measure daily sales velocity: how fast the product actually sells, measured over time. Use Shopify order history to spot velocity, slow movers and seasonal spikes, and review weekly.
Measure total lead time: the full duration from paying your supplier to stock arriving at your warehouse or 3PL, including production, shipping and customs clearance.
Set a safety stock buffer to cover sales spikes or freight delays so you keep selling.
Compute: Reorder Point = (Daily Sales Velocity x Total Lead Time in days) + Safety Stock.
Apply the source's worked example: 50 units/day velocity, 60 days total lead time, 500 units safety stock gives a reorder point of 3,500 units. When inventory hits that level, reorder.
Feed weekly performance and stock-level reviews into the reorder plan, and communicate them to suppliers before problems appear.
caveats: The example numbers are illustrative inputs, not benchmarks; your velocity, lead time and safety stock must come from your own data.
The source attributes a major stockout and lost sales to having no forecasting system in place — treat the formula as a discipline, not a one-time calculation.

cards.title: Build a Weekly Forecasting Rhythm Even as a Solo Operator
cards.summary: Forecasting is not an afterthought: assign someone or a weekly ritual to review velocity, lead times and stock so demand spikes don't leave you sold out for months.
cards.use_when: You need a repeatable operating cadence to keep sourced products in stock and profitable, whether you are solo or have a small team.
steps: Create a simple system that forces a performance and stock-level review every single week.
Include daily sales velocity, total lead time and safety stock in the same sheet you use for the reorder point calculation.
Communicate stock and forecast positions to suppliers proactively, before problems appear.
If possible, designate one person focused purely on operations and planning rather than splitting the role.
Start planning the next shipment when the current one lands, since production plus transit can consume 50-70 days in total.

Treat the failure mode as a planning failure, not bad luck: the source describes a demand spike to $200,000/day sales followed by a sellout, months-long lead times and nearly two months unable to fulfill orders.
The source believes a dedicated operations/planning focus could have made that business 30-40% bigger — its own retrospective estimate, not a universal figure.
caveats: The 30-40% upside figure is the source's retrospective opinion about its own business, not a benchmark for yours.
The source states you do not need a full team to start — discipline and a weekly cadence suffice initially.

cards.title: Keep Your Product Factory-Ready Before You Message Suppliers
cards.summary: Most sourcing problems start with the product definition, not the factory: unclear specs cause suppliers to guess, cut corners and produce inconsistent stock.
cards.use_when: You are defining a new product or fixing recurring inconsistency across reorders before you start supplier outreach.
steps: Get crystal clear on every specification before contacting any supplier. The source's own early experience: a blanket shipment arrived with three different shades of gray and different weights in the same SKU because no spec sheet had been sent.
Reframe the failure as your own: factories do not see your brand the way you do; they optimize for throughput and efficiency, so undefined details default to whatever is easiest for them.
Build the tech pack described in these cards as the single source of truth for materials, measurements, colorways, trims and packaging.
Treat inconsistency across reorders as a specification problem until proven otherwise.
Once specs are defined, supplier sourcing becomes easier because suppliers cannot take shortcuts and you are no longer guessing.
caveats: The three-shades-of-gray incident is the source's personal example, used to illustrate the cost of unclear specs, not a typical defect rate.
The source insists a tech pack is not optional for serious product quality — an opinion, not an industry-wide mandate.

cards.title: Protect IP and Build Long-Term Supplier Partnerships
cards.summary: Treat reliable suppliers as partners with early forecasts, on-time payment and repeat business, while keeping tech packs, artwork and source files on your side.
cards.use_when: You have selected a final supplier and are scaling volume, renewing terms, or assessing how much information to share.
steps: Share forecasts early so the factory can plan capacity; factories prioritize their best clients first, so become one.
Pay on time and reward good performance with repeat business rather than constantly switching on marginal price differences.
Keep original tech packs, artwork and source files on your side — do not rely on the factory holding your IP.
Once at volume, get a manufacturing agreement signed and register all your trademarks.
Treat the relationship as a partnership in negotiation as well: the source warns that squeezing a supplier too hard results in cheaper materials, skipped QC or slower timelines.
caveats: The source does not specify contract terms or jurisdictions; get local legal advice for manufacturing agreements and trademark registration.
The advice to keep files in-house is the source's stated practice, not a legal guarantee of protection.

18-COG / sourcing Goes here. A comprehensive guide to e-commerce product sourcing and supply chain management. Covers creating Tech Packs, vetting suppliers (Alibaba vs. sourcing agents), understanding True Landed Costs, managing freight (Air vs. Sea) and 3PL fulfillment, executing quality control (QC) checks, and calculating inventory reorder points. Not here. • Team management, hiring, or internal business operations -> 21-OPS • SEO or organic search strategies -> 15-SEO

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the entire lifecycle of physical product sourcing for e-commerce, moving from product definition (Tech Packs) through manufacturing, freight, 3PL logistics, and inventory forecasting. modules: [COG] topics: [sourcing, supply chain, Tech Packs, supplier vetting, landed cost, freight forwarding, 3PL, inventory forecasting, quality control] tier: 2 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. product definition / utilizing a "Tech Pack" as a strict product blueprint containing exact materials, GSM, trims, Pantone codes, and measurements to prevent factory shortcuts; supplier vetting / using Alibaba to shortlist 10-15 verified suppliers, executing video calls to spot red flags, and progressing through strike-off samples to pre-production and final production samples; True Landed Cost / calculating the actual unit cost by factoring in the X-factory price plus freight, duties, taxes, insurance, warehousing, and 3PL pick/pack fees; freight and logistics / blending Air freight (fast, expensive) with Sea freight (slow, 30-40 days) to balance inventory speed and margin; quality control / mandating a $200 third-party QC inspection before the container leaves the factory to prevent receiving damaged stock; 3PL management / selecting third-party logistics partners based on accuracy, speed, communication, and scalability, emphasizing the need for proactive communication during Q4 surges; inventory forecasting / tracking Daily Sales Velocity and Lead Times to determine exact reorder points, calculating it as: (Daily Sales Velocity x Total Lead Time) + Safety Stock.

Look for.

The Tech Pack Requirement: The explicit instruction to never manufacture a product without a detailed Tech Pack (blueprint) outlining exact GSM, Pantone colors, trims, and packaging folds, preventing the factory from making cheap assumptions.

True Landed Cost: The definition that the "X-factory price" is just the beginning, and profitability must be calculated using "Landed Cost" (Cost of Goods + Freight + Duties + 3PL fulfillment + Platform fees).

The Pre-Shipment QC Check: The hard rule to hire a third-party Quality Control inspector for ~$200 to check random units and carton weights before the container leaves the port, as problems cannot be fixed once the stock is on the water.

The Reorder Point Formula: The specific calculation for when to reorder stock: Reorder Point = (Daily Sales Velocity x Total Lead Time in days) + Safety Stock.

Skip. Plugs for the Daily Mentor program and the story about the Oodie selling out during COVID unless used to define forecasting.

Scope mix. 100% baseline (standard supply chain and sourcing execution). Volume. ~350 words.

The biggest reasons brands go out of business isn't marketing. [music] It's actually sourcing. Sourcing is difficult. You're dealing with late suppliers, wrong samples, shifting prices, and constant delays. I've lived through it all. After building the Udie, past $850 million in sales, I can tell you that operations is the hardest part of e-commerce, but also the most rewarding once it's done right. That's why today I'm going to give you an ultimate product guide [music] and sourcing guide and operations guide. This is the exact kind of guide that I wish I had when I started. You'll learn how to make your product factory ready. Find and vet suppliers, negotiate prices, and build systems that keep your margins strong and your brand in control. Let's start with the foundation. How to make your product truly factory ready before you even message a supplier. Chapter one, product definition. Most sourcing problems don't start at the factory. They start with the product itself. [music] If you aren't crystal clear on specifications of your product, you're asking for trouble. Suppliers will guess, cut corners, and you'll end up with inconsistent stock, wasted cash, and frustrated customers. Back when I started calming blankets, I remember getting our first big shipment after weeks of waiting. We opened the containers and instantly realized something was wrong. The blankets were all different. Same skew, same fabric, but three completely different shades of gray and different weights. They didn't mess up. We did. We had never given the factory a clear spec sheet. [music] They just made assumptions. It was an expensive mistake that could have been avoided with one proper thing, a proper tech pack. [music] A tech pack is your product's blueprint. It's the single document that defines how your product should be built. From materials all the way to packaging. Without it, every reorder becomes a gamble. You might get lucky once, but you'll never build consistency with your product without a tech pack. When I first learned about tech packs, I realized how many variables I'd been leaving open for the supplier. The thickness of the fabric, the exact drawstring length, even how the packaging was folded. Every one of those details matters because factories don't see your brand the way you do. They care about throughput and efficiency. If something isn't defined, they'll choose whatever is easiest for them, and they'll try to sneak things in. So, if you're serious about product quality, your tech pack isn't optional. Here's what a solid tech pack should definitely include. Detailed product drawings or photos from every angle. Exact materials and finishes, including GSM, trims, and hardware. Measurements for every size or variant, colorways, and pantone codes, label, packaging, and care instructions, clear product name, version, and date. If you're not a designer, that's fine. Hire someone that is. On Upwork, you can find experienced product designers who will build your tech pack for $200. It's worth [music] every cent. You can also use tools like Figma, Canva, or Notion templates to keep your specs always up to date. When you reach this stage, sourcing becomes way easier. You're no longer guessing and suppliers can't take shortcuts. You're in control of the process. So, now your product is truly factory ready. Let's talk about how to actually find the right suppliers to bring it to life. Chapter two, suppliers and sampling. This is where sourcing becomes real because a good supplier will make you more money for years and a bad one can sink you in a single order. So, how do we vet and find suppliers? Most founders start on Alibaba, which is totally fine. It's still the easiest way to get a feel for pricing, materials, and minimum order quantities, but you have to treat it like research, not a final decision. Don't just click the first link that looks professional. You need to verify everything. The first step is building a short list. Search by your exact product type. Filter by verified suppliers and trade assurance and message at least 10 to 15 factories. You'll lose some along the way and that's fine. You're testing for responsiveness, professionalism, and whether they produce similar products before. Once you've shortlisted a few, get on a video call. Ask them to walk you through their facility or show you some sample products. You'll quickly spot some red flags such as vague answers, poor communication, or someone clearly operating from their living room. Then comes the verification step. check how long they've been active, their export countries, and request documents like their ISO or BSCI certifications. Now, if you're planning on scaling using a sourcing agent or like a platform like Quimma or Easy IMAX, they'll inspect factories in person for you. It's also worth diversifying outside of China depending on your product type and your age of business. If you're an older business, maybe you can consider other countries like Vietnam, India, and Turkey. But you need to make sure you're at the right size to do this. Now, a good supplier relationship starts with clarity. Send them your tech pack and ask for quotes that include things like your unit cost for each skew or variation, your minimum order quantity, your lead time to manufacture, and packaging details and payment terms. Now, we've got that covered. This is where sampling comes into play. When you find a few potential suppliers, get samples from all of them. It's not just about quality. It's about communication and reliability. who follows instructions the best, who sends updates without being asked who can match your tech pack precisely. Start with a strike off or small test sample for materials and prints, and once that's approved, move to a pre-production sample, which should match your tech pack perfectly. Treat this as your gold standard. When you move to bulk, this is the reference you'll compare against. For apparel, this is also where you confirm grading. Make sure your sizes, small, medium, and large, scale correctly. Get multiple samples in the pre-production round to confirm proportions. Once you're happy, keep one sample inhouse and then keep one of these samples in the factory for reference. When you've chosen your final supplier, move to a production sample. This is a final test built right before mass production. If it doesn't match your pre-production standard, don't proceed. Building long-term supplier relationships. A good supplier isn't just a vendor, they're a partner. Once you find someone reliable, treat them like part of your team. Share your forecasts early, pay on time, and reward good performance with repeat business. Factories will always prioritize their best clients first. Just become one of them. And protect your product as you scale. Always keep your original tech packs, artwork, and source files on your side. Once you're at volume, get a manufacturing agreement signed and register all of your trademarks. When you follow this process completely, you turn chaos to control. You'll know who you're working with, what to expect, and how to keep your standards high every single order. So, now that you understand how to find a reliable supplier and what a production ready sample looks like, chapter three, price,QS, terms, and POSOS. You can have a great product and reliable supplier, but if you don't understand your numbers, you're building on sand. I see this time and time again with founders designing an amazing product with great branding, but everything falls apart when production begins because they never account for pricing or profit properly. Even larger companies make this mistake. They rush from design straight into manufacturing without ever checking if the numbers actually make sense. Let's say we designed an Udie with a built-in heated pockets and Bluetooth temperature controls. Something crazy. That might be something that people would line up for and we want to sell it for say $50, but that product might cost $40 or something to make up. Meaning that I'd have to sell the product for $200. That instantly kills the idea. Understanding your costs upfront is what decides whether your product is even viable. Understanding true unit cost. When you're new to manufacturing, it's easy to think you're making great margins until you realize how many hidden costs are actually under the quote. The number your supplier gives you is rarely the full picture. That's the X factory price, [music] meaning it only covers the physical production. But the second that the product leaves the factory, a whole new layer of costs begin. There's freight, which can fluctuate wildly depending on fuel and global shipping rates. Then duties and taxes, which differ from country and product type. You've also got insurance, warehousing, packaging, and fulfillment fees. each one nibbling at your profits until what looked like 60% margin turns into 20%. When I first started scaling my dog bed business, what seemed like a very very profitable business, all of these costs started to add up and it was nowhere near as profitable as I thought. That's when I learned the concept of landed cost. The total cost of your product once it's in your warehouse and ready to sell. It's the only number that really matters with sourcing. Here's the thing. Most people don't do this math until it's too late. They make decisions on what feels affordable, not what's actually profitable. This is why it's important to build out a detailed spreadsheet breaking down everything: product, freight, packaging, duties, taxes, warehousing, platform fees, transaction costs, and payment transfer fees. If you want to understand your landed cost for customers, you'll also need courier fees. If you need help building the spreadsheet, just go to Chat TBT and prompt it asking for all of these hidden costs and then fill out the template. Alternatively, you can join Daily Mentor. We've got so many templates like this. So, when you know your real cost per unit, you can start making smarter choices everywhere else. Marketing spend, ad testing, even offer strategy, pricing, and negotiation. Once you understand your costs, it's time to focus on how pricing and negotiation really works. Most founders chase the lowest possible unit cost, thinking it's the key to profit, and end up sitting in warehouses full of unsold products. Sure, they saved $2 a unit, but they killed their cash flow in the process. Because you see, early on, flexibility is worth more than margin. Paying slightly more per unit gives you room to test, pivot, and adjust without overcommitting. Your first few production runs might not be about maximizing profit. They might be about learning, such as how fast does the stock sell, how consistent is quality, and where delays happen. Once you know those answers, that's when you can negotiate confidently. And remember, negotiation isn't just about price. It's about partnership. If you squeeze a supplier too hard, they'll make up the difference somewhere else, such as cheaper materials, skipped quality control, or sometimes even slower timelines. Factories have margins, too. And when they're under pressure, your brand usually pays for it later. Good negotiation means balancing what works for both sides. Now, no factory will ever lower their price or offer better payment terms unless they know that you have options. That's why it's smart to get quotes or samples from at least one other supplier. It keeps the conversation honest and gives you leverage without hostility. Be transparent about your goal. Share your forecast and show them your serious about scaling. Now that you know your margins and have your deal locked in, it's time to learn how to move that product. And that's where freight and fulfillment come in next. Chapter four, freight, customs, and fulfillment. Getting your product from the factory floor to your hands of your customers without losing your sanity or your profit can be very, very painful. Logistics is the bloodstream of your business. Every day your inventory sits idle, it's burning cash. Every time you touch it, it's burning cash. The faster and cleaner you can move your stock through the supply chain, the stronger your cash flow and the calmer your business will feel. Freight forwarders and planning lead times. There are really only two ways to move your product. Air or C. Air is fast and expensive, which is perfect for small or urgent batches or if you've got a tiny product. C is slower but dramatically cheaper. It's what keeps your margins healthy once you're scaling. Most successful brands use a hybrid strategy. Air freight, a small batch to start selling quickly, then follow up with C shipments to restock at lower cost. But this really depends on your product size and weight. For small items, a mix works well. For larger or heavier items, C freight is almost always the best option. But moving stock isn't just about picking a transport method. It's about planning lead times backwards. Freight isn't instant. Sea can take 30 to 40 days doortodoor. Air might take 7 to 10 and production itself can often add another 20 or 30 days. That means that if you wait until you are nearly out of stock to reorder, you're already too late. Start planning your next shipment the moment your current one lands. The biggest reason brands panic ship or run out of stock isn't bad luck, it's just bad forecasting. From the moment your PO is signed, your countdown begins. You need visibility from factory to warehouse at all times. That's where freight forwarders come in. These companies manage the complex stuff for you. Booking containers, handling customs, and coordinating delivery to your warehouse. A good forwarder will update you before problems happen and help you navigate global delays. If you've ever tried to handle shipping yourself, you know it's chaos. Different time zones, customs forms, endless email chains. A strong forwarder simplifies all of that. They'll quote you based on route, wait, and deadlights. And more importantly, they'll tell you what's realistic. And again, don't always chase the cheapest rate. The cheapest freight forer might leave your goods sitting at a port for weeks and fill a container instead. Finally, before that container leaves the factory, book your final inspection. This is your last chance to catch mistakes before they multiply. A $200 QC check, quality control check, can save $20,000 in damage or inconsistent stock in that last check stage. Your QC agent will test random units, check measurements, verify packaging, labeling, and carton weight. And they'll take photos of everything. [music] They'll flag even small inconsistencies that could become massive issues later. If they find problems, the factory can fix them before the shipment leaves. Once it's on the water, it's just too late. You need to think beyond just product quality and more about protecting your reputation and customer experience. Think of it like insurance, a small cost that keeps your entire operation safe. You approve or reject the shipment based on that report and only release final payment once everything passes. Fulfillment and 3PLs. If all goes smoothly and your goods arrive, your job still isn't finished. It's now just shifted from production to delivery. Disorganization can kill brands at this step. You need to learn more about 3PL's. A 3PL, also known as third party logistics provider, is the bridge between your factory and your customers. They store, pick, pack, and ship your orders, manage returns, and often integrate directly with Shopify or your warehouse management tools. However, the difference between a good 3PL and a bad one can make or break your experience with e-commerce. When we were scaling the Udy, fulfillment became our biggest threat overnight. During one of our Q4, we were forecasting record numbers, $45, $50 million in sales, and everything looked perfect until one of our 3PL collapsed under the pressure. We lost tens of millions in potential revenue and even ended up in the news because customers thought we were scamming them. It was one of the hardest lessons that I've ever learned. That experience made me realize how critical fulfillment partners are. You can do everything right, product, marketing, sourcing, and still lose it all if your logistics partner fails you. So, how do you pick the right one? Don't just compare prices or promises. Ask questions that really expose how they operate, such as accuracy. What's their error rate on orders shipped? Speed. How fast do they process during peak volume and how do they do that? Communication. Who's your direct contact when problems [music] actually hit? Scalability. How have they handled previous Q4 surges for other brands? And never skip going to visit their warehouse to see how it all operates. Once you've seen two or three, you realize who the true players actually are. You also want to ask them how do they handle returns, damages, and restocks. Do they flag issues proactively or wait for you to notice? Those answers tell you who will protect your brand when orders start flying. Our coaches at Daily Mentor always hammer home that fulfillment isn't a set and forget system. It's a living part of your business. The best operators track inventory turnover weekly, maintain shared dashboards with their warehouses, and hold monthly reviews with their 3PL partners. These habits prevent the exact disaster we went through. Once you built a setup like this, your logistics should start to feel very, very calm. And that's the goal, predictable, repeatable, and reliable. When fulfillment runs on autopilot and nothing feels urgent, that's when you know it's working. Next, let's look at the final piece of the puzzle. Forecasting, cash flow, and reordering. How do you actually keep up this whole system running without ever running out of stock again? [music] Chapter 5, forecasting and planning. You might think the hardest part of sourcing is over once your product is shipping smoothly and orders are being fulfilled. But that's actually where most brands slip. Everything you've built up to this point, your supplier relationships, your logistics, your product quality, only matters if you can keep it consistent. A lot of founders treat forecasting like an afterthought, but it's one of the most important parts of sourcing. Because sourcing isn't just about finding great products. [music] It's about keeping them in stock, profitable, and moving through your supply chain. If you followed everything up to now, this is the final step that ties it all together. This part will decide whether your sourcing process scales or collapses. The real cost of poor planning. Back in the early days of the Udie, I thought we had it all figured out. Our products were selling fast, ads were converting, and everything looked like it was working perfectly. But then co hit. I remember watching sales skyrocket overnight, $200,000 days back to back and thinking we'd hit the jackpot. But I didn't realize how big the demand spike would be. Within a week, we were completely sold out. It doesn't sound like a problem, right? Wrong. We had zero stock, monthsl long production lead times, and no forecasting system in place to keep catching up. For almost two months, we couldn't fulfill orders, couldn't capitalize on demand, and lost millions in potential sales. Worse, it damaged the momentum. Customers got frustrated, and our performance tanked. That experience taught me one thing. If you're not forecasting, you're gambling. You can't grow what you can't plan. That experience forced me to completely rethink forecasting and operations. We didn't just fail to reorder. We failed to plan at all. There was no one inside the business dedicated to looking ahead, checking lead times, or adjusting our forecast regularly. And that's why we missed the moment. Looking back, if we had someone focused purely on operations and planning, the Udie could have been 30, 40% bigger. But the truth is, you don't need a full team right away to get this right. You just need discipline. Whether you're a solo founder or have a small crew, you can still build a forecasting rhythm that protects your sourcing. Create a simple system that forces you to review performance and stock levels every single week and communicate these with your suppliers before problems appear. This goes handinhand with what I mentioned on credibility. Here's a simple version of what this forecasting sheet should look like. It should have daily sales velocity, such as how fast your products actually sell, measured over time. This shows how quickly inventory is moving. You should have lead time, how long it takes from paying your supplier to the stock arriving at your warehouse or 3PL, including production, shipping, and clearance. Then you also need to have safety stock, which is basically your insurance buffer. When sales spike or freight gets delayed, this keeps you selling. Then you can just use this simple equation. Your reorder point equals the daily sales velocity times total lead time plus safety sold. For example, if you sell 50 units a day, your total lead time is 60 days and you keep 500 units as safety stock. Your reorder point is 3500 units. When your inventory hits that level, it's time to reorder. Shopify already gives you almost everything you need. Use your order history to spot sales velocity, slow movers, and seasonal spikes. Make sure to check those insights weekly and feed them into your reorder plan. If this video helped you, go check out all of the mistakes that I made in this video on the screen. And make sure you like and subscribe. Peace.
